questions.title: Germ-layer origin of epithelial tissue
questions.question: Epithelial tissue is derived from which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ectoderm gives rise to some epithelia — skin, and the oral and anal canal linings — but not all of them.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Endoderm gives rise to the gut tube's lining and its glandular derivatives, but not to every epithelium in the body.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mesoderm gives rise to endothelium and mesothelium, but not to the surface epithelia derived from ectoderm and endoderm.
explanations.D: Correct. Epithelial tissue arises from all three germ layers depending on the site: ectoderm for skin and the oral/anal canal linings, endoderm for the gut tube and its glandular outgrowths, and mesoderm for endothelium and mesothelium. A question naming one germ layer as the source of epithelium is testing whether a student mistakenly generalises from the most familiar example, the ectodermal skin, to every epithelium in the body. Recognising all three origins is the foundation for later linking a specific epithelium to its embryological derivation.

questions.learning_objective: State that epithelium can derive from ectoderm, mesoderm or endoderm depending on the site, rather than from one germ layer alone.

questions.title: Naming a gland by its branched duct
questions.question: Which of the following is the term for a gland with a branched duct?

explanations.A: Correct. A compound gland is defined by having a branched duct system — the duct divides before reaching the secretory units, as in the pancreas and the major salivary glands. This is a separate classifying axis from whether a gland has a duct at all (exocrine, endocrine or mixed), and from the shape of its secretory units (tubular, acinar or alveolar). Recognising duct branching as the specific criterion for "compound" prevents it being confused with either of those other two classification axes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Coiled" describes the shape of a secretory unit (as in a coiled tubular gland such as a sweat gland), not the branching of its duct.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A simple gland has a single, unbranched duct reaching the surface — the opposite of the branched-duct criterion the question asks for.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Simple branched gland" describes a gland with one duct serving several secretory units, which is a different (and less commonly examined) category from a compound gland's branched duct.

questions.learning_objective: Classify a gland as simple or compound from whether its duct branches.

questions.title: Cell of origin of macrophages
questions.question: Which cell is the origin of macrophages?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Undifferentiated mesenchymal cells are a tissue-resident stem-cell population that can form fibroblasts and other connective-tissue cells, not the direct precursor of the tissue macrophage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. B lymphocytes are a separate lineage of the immune system, committed to antibody production, not to phagocytic macrophage function.
explanations.C: Correct. Circulating blood monocytes, once they leave the bloodstream and enter a tissue, differentiate into tissue macrophages (given site-specific names such as Kupffer cells in the liver or microglia in the CNS). This monocyte-to-macrophage transition is the standard route by which the body maintains its tissue phagocyte population. Note this printed key is a plurality only — 96 of 220 respondents (44%) — so the item is worth a second look even though the underlying physiology is standard.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adipoblasts are the precursor of adipocytes (fat-storing cells), an entirely different differentiation pathway from the monocyte-macrophage lineage.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the blood monocyte as the origin of the tissue macrophage.

questions.title: Fusion of primary lysosomes with undigested remnants
questions.question: Which of the following is the term for the fusion of primary lysosomes with undigested remnants?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A heterolysosome is a primary lysosome fused with a phagosome (material taken in from outside the cell) — a specific type of secondary lysosome named by what it fused with, not the end state of undigested remnants.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A multivesicular body is a primary lysosome fused with a pinocytic vesicle (fluid taken in from outside), again named by what it fused with rather than by its undigested end state.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An autolysosome is a primary lysosome fused with the cell's own worn-out organelles, a third named-by-origin secondary lysosome — not the end-state term the question asks for.
explanations.D: Correct. Whichever secondary lysosome forms — heterolysosome, multivesicular body or autolysosome — what is left undigested after its digestive work becomes a residual body. The residual body is either discharged from the cell by exocytosis or retained as lipofuscin, the age pigment that accumulates particularly in non-dividing cells such as cardiac muscle and neurons. This end-state terminology is distinct from the three origin-based names of secondary lysosomes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the residual body as the undigested end-state of any secondary lysosome.

questions.title: Organelle handling drug detoxification
questions.question: Enzymes used for detoxification of some drugs are attached to which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) is a membranous organelle of branching, ribosome-free tubules concerned with lipid and steroid synthesis, and it also carries the enzymes that detoxify drugs — well developed in cells such as hepatocytes that do both jobs. On light microscopy it does not stain as a distinct structure but, where abundant, gives the cytoplasm an acidophilic tinge, distinguishing it from the basophilic cytoplasm of protein-exporting cells. Its lack of bound ribosomes, continuous with rough ER, is the structural feature that separates it from the rough ER named in option D.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lysosomes digest material that has been taken into the cell or worn-out organelles; drug detoxification is a distinct SER-based function, not a lysosomal one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mitochondria generate ATP through oxidative metabolism; they are not the site of drug-detoxifying enzymes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rough endoplasmic reticulum, studded with ribosomes, synthesises and segregates protein for export — a different job from the ribosome-free smooth ER's drug-detoxification role.

questions.learning_objective: Identify smooth endoplasmic reticulum as the organelle carrying drug-detoxification enzymes.

questions.title: Structure responsible for the cell's immune function
questions.question: Immunity is one of the functions of which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. The cell coat, or glycocalyx, is a loose meshwork of polysaccharide fibrils extending from the outer surface of the plasma membrane. Among its functions is a role in immune recognition — the glycocalyx contributes antigenic surface markers and mediates cell-to-cell recognition, which is why it is described as having an immunity function. This surface location is what distinguishes its function from the intracellular organelles listed as distractors.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lysosomes are digestive organelles that break down material taken into the cell; they are not the surface structure responsible for immune recognition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The nucleus houses and regulates the cell's genetic material; it plays no direct surface-recognition role in immunity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ribosomes synthesise protein; they have no direct role in the surface-recognition function being tested here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the glycocalyx (cell coat) as the surface structure with a role in immune recognition.

questions.title: Direction the palm faces during pronation
questions.question: If you are asked to put the arm in pronation, the palm of the hand should be facing which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Anterior is where the palm faces before pronation, at the anatomical-position starting point — the opposite of where pronation carries it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lateral is not the plane pronation moves the palm through; pronation is a rotation of the radius, not an abduction movement.
explanations.C: Correct. Pronation is the forearm movement that rotates the radius across the ulna. Starting from the anatomical position, where the palm faces anteriorly, pronation carries the palm to face posteriorly. Stating this direction correctly depends on holding the anatomical position as the fixed starting reference, which is exactly what a student who answers this wrong has usually lost track of.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Superiorly describes an up/down (vertical) direction, not the rotational movement of the forearm that pronation produces.

questions.learning_objective: State which way the palm faces after pronation, from the anatomical position.

questions.title: Direction the sole faces during inversion
questions.question: In inversion, the plantar surface of the foot is facing which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Down" describes the plantar surface's normal resting orientation while standing, not the direction inversion turns it toward.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lateral is the direction eversion (inversion's opposite) turns the sole toward, not inversion.
explanations.C: Correct. Inversion is a subtalar-joint movement of the foot that tilts the sole (plantar surface) to face medially, toward the opposite foot. Its opposite, eversion, turns the sole to face laterally. Keeping this movement pair distinct from the forearm's supination/pronation pair — a different joint entirely — is the main source of confusion this item is testing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Up" is not a direction the plantar surface faces during either inversion or eversion; both movements tilt it sideways (medially or laterally), not vertically.

questions.learning_objective: State which way the plantar surface of the foot faces during inversion.

questions.title: Newly formed bone at the end of the diaphysis
questions.question: Which of the following is the term for the newly formed bone at the end of the diaphysis?

explanations.A: Correct. A long bone is a diaphysis (shaft) with an epiphysis at each end; the metaphysis is the region of newly formed bone where the diaphysis and epiphysis meet, the site of longitudinal growth in a growing bone. This growth-zone role is what the distractors below, which name the epiphyses themselves, fail to capture.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The upper epiphysis is the bone end itself, not the newly forming zone where diaphysis meets epiphysis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lower epiphysis is likewise the bone end, not the growth-zone term the question asks for.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Naming both epiphyses still describes the bone ends rather than the metaphyseal growth zone between shaft and end.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the metaphysis as the newly formed bone region between diaphysis and epiphysis.

questions.title: Covering of a long bone's articular surface
questions.question: By which of the following is the articular surface of a long bone covered?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Endosteum lines the internal (medullary) surface of bone, not the external articular surface.
explanations.B: Correct. Hyaline cartilage, the most common and glassy-translucent of the three cartilage types, covers the articular (joint) surface of a long bone, providing a smooth, low-friction surface for movement. It is the structural template referenced when comparing the other cartilage types, and articular cartilage is one of the few hyaline sites that is never replaced by bone even into adulthood.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Periosteum covers the external, non-articular shaft surface of a long bone; it stops short of the articular surface itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Synovial membrane lines the inside of the joint capsule, not the bone's own articular surface, and it does not cover cartilage.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hyaline cartilage as the covering of a long bone's articular surface.

questions.title: Anatomical term for the area near the foot
questions.question: Which of the following is the anatomical term given to the area near the foot?

explanations.A: Correct. Caudal is a directional term meaning toward the tail (coccygeal) end of the body; in standing human anatomical position this corresponds to the inferior direction, toward the feet. It is a direction, applicable along the whole body axis, not a fixed named region.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cranial means toward the head end — the opposite direction from the one the question describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Proximal means closer to the root/trunk attachment of a limb, a different axis of measurement from the head-to-tail (cranial-caudal) one being tested here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ventral means toward the front (anterior) surface of the body, a different axis again from the cranial-caudal one.

questions.learning_objective: Identify caudal as the anatomical term for the direction toward the feet/tail end.

questions.title: Body region not supplied by spinal nerves
questions.question: Which of the following is the part of the body that is not supplied by spinal nerves?

explanations.A: Correct. Spinal nerves supply the trunk and all four limbs. The head and neck's sensory and motor supply comes instead from the twelve cranial nerves, making the head the one major body region a spinal nerve does not directly reach (upper cervical spinal nerves do contribute a strip of posterior scalp skin, a genuine nuance beyond the exam's stated answer). This cranial-versus-spinal distinction is exactly what the item is testing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lower limb is supplied by the lumbosacral plexus, formed from lumbar and sacral spinal nerves — it is not the exception the question describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The trunk is supplied segmentally by thoracic and lumbar spinal nerves — again not the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The upper limb is supplied by the brachial plexus, formed from cervical and upper thoracic spinal nerves — also not the exception.

questions.learning_objective: State that the head is supplied by cranial, not spinal, nerves, while the trunk and limbs are supplied by spinal nerves.

questions.title: The one vein carrying oxygenated blood
questions.question: Which of the following is the only vein that carries oxygenated blood?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The inferior vena cava carries deoxygenated systemic venous blood back to the right atrium, like every other systemic vein.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The portal vein carries deoxygenated (though nutrient-rich) venous blood from the gut, spleen and pancreas to the liver, not oxygenated blood.
explanations.C: Correct. Every vein in the adult systemic circulation carries deoxygenated blood back to the heart. The four pulmonary veins are the sole postnatal exception: they carry newly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium, which is why they are singled out as "the only vein" carrying oxygenated blood.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior vena cava, like the inferior vena cava, carries deoxygenated systemic venous blood to the right atrium.

questions.learning_objective: Name the pulmonary veins as the exception to "veins carry deoxygenated blood."

questions.title: Structure not part of the small intestine
questions.question: Which of the following is the structure that is not part of the small intestine?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The duodenum is the first of the three small-intestine segments.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ileum is the third and final small-intestine segment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The jejunum is the second small-intestine segment, between duodenum and ileum.
explanations.D: Correct. The small intestine consists specifically of the duodenum, jejunum and ileum. The vermiform appendix is a blind-ended diverticulum off the caecum, the first part of the large intestine — so it is a large-intestine structure, not part of the small intestine, even though it sits close to the ileocaecal junction.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the vermiform appendix as a large-intestine structure, distinct from the small intestine's three segments.

questions.title: Peripheral membrane protein function
questions.question: Which of the following is present in the cell membrane?

options.A: Peripheral proteins which may function as enzymes or hormone receptors
options.B: Integral proteins which are necessary for the transport of respiratory gases
options.C: Lipid channels through which protein and lipid substances can diffuse easily
options.D: Two layers of proteins one is hydrophilic and the other is hydrophobic

explanations.A: Correct. Cell membrane proteins are classed as integral (embedded in or spanning the lipid bilayer) or peripheral (attached loosely to one membrane surface, not embedded in the bilayer). Peripheral proteins commonly function as enzymes or as hormone/signal receptors at the membrane surface. Respiratory gases (O2, CO2) actually diffuse directly through the lipid bilayer rather than needing a dedicated integral transport protein, which is the flaw in option B.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Respiratory gases cross the membrane by simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer itself; they do not require a dedicated integral transport protein the way glucose or ions do.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Lipid channels" through which both protein and lipid substances diffuse are not a real feature of the plasma membrane — the membrane is a lipid bilayer with embedded proteins, not a channel system for lipids and proteins together.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The membrane's phospholipid bilayer, not a protein bilayer, is the structure with a hydrophilic side and a hydrophobic side; describing two protein layers this way misattributes the amphipathic property.

questions.learning_objective: State that peripheral membrane proteins, as distinct from integral ones, characteristically function as enzymes or receptors at the membrane surface.
